concept.body: The fold test is the whole definition: a line of symmetry is a fold along which the two halves land EXACTLY on each other — every edge on an edge, every corner on a corner. One overhanging corner disqualifies the fold.

explanationVariants: The equilateral triangle folds perfectly along the line from each vertex to the opposite side's midpoint — 3 vertices, 3 lines.
It's the regular 3-gon, so the n-lines rule gives exactly 3.

widget.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does an EQUILATERAL triangle have?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is only the vertical fold — but all three sides are equal, so the fold from EACH vertex works: 3 lines.
6 double-counts each fold from both ends — vertex-to-midpoint is one line. The regular 3-gon has exactly 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Regular 3-gon: 3 lines, one through each vertex.

steps.body: Point a reflection back at its own figure. A shape has **line symmetry** when some reflection maps the shape **exactly onto itself** — the mirror line is its **line of symmetry**. The physical test: fold along the line; the two halves must match perfectly, edge for edge.

widget.prompt: Tap every letter that has a VERTICAL line of symmetry (a fold down the middle matches left half to right half).

hotspots.label: B
hotspots.feedback: B's mirror line is HORIZONTAL — fold top onto bottom and it matches. A vertical fold pairs the flat left spine with the round right bumps: no match.

hotspots.label: R
hotspots.feedback: R has no line of symmetry at all — the leg kicks out one way, and no fold in any direction matches the halves.

widget.missFeedback: Fold each letter down its vertical middle in your head — both halves must land exactly on each other.
widget.successFeedback: A and H pass the vertical fold. (H even passes a horizontal one too — two lines.)

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents gf line symmetry.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for gf line symmetry must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines gf line symmetry.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

predict.prompt: A vertical line of symmetry means a fold down the middle matches the left half to the right. Which of these letters has one?
predict.reveal: A. Fold it down the middle and the two halves land exactly on each other. L and R have no fold that works anywhere — a shape either has a mirror that maps it onto itself or it does not, and "nearly" is not a kind of symmetry.

explanationVariants: A non-square rectangle has exactly 2 lines: the vertical and horizontal midlines. The diagonals FAIL the fold test — folding along one lands long sides on short sides.
Try the diagonal fold: the corners overhang instead of matching. Only the two midlines swap the rectangle onto itself.

widget.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a (non-square) rectangle have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 counts the diagonals — but fold a rectangle along a diagonal and the long side lands on a SHORT side. Diagonal mirrors belong to the square; the rectangle keeps only its 2 midlines.
There are two midline folds, not one: top-onto-bottom AND left-onto-right both match perfectly.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The two midlines — vertical and horizontal — and nothing else: 2.

steps.body: Counting lines is a search over mirror candidates: midlines, diagonals, vertex-to-opposite-edge folds. **Regular polygons are maximal**: a regular n-gon has exactly **n** lines of symmetry (through each vertex for odd n; alternating vertex-lines and edge-midpoint-lines for even n).

explanationVariants: A regular n-gon has n lines: for the pentagon, one through each vertex to the opposite edge's midpoint — 5.
Rotate the pentagon a fifth of a turn and the "vertical" fold becomes a new fold. Five vertices, five folds.

widget.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a REGULAR pentagon have?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 is just the vertical fold — but the pentagon is regular, so every vertex-to-opposite-edge fold works the same way. Five vertices, five lines.
10 double-counts: a fold through a vertex and the opposite edge midpoint is ONE line, not two. Regular n-gon: exactly n lines — here 5.

steps.body: Two ends of the spectrum: a scalene triangle has **zero** lines (no fold ever matches unequal sides), while the extreme case is the circle — EVERY diameter is a mirror. Symmetry count is a fingerprint: it separates shapes that otherwise look alike.

widget.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?

options.label: Infinitely many
options.feedback: Any diameter folds the circle onto itself, and there's a diameter at every angle: no finite count survives.

options.label: Just 1, the line you can see drawn
options.feedback: Whatever single line you pick, tilt it a degree about the center — the new line folds the circle just as perfectly. One can't be the total.

options.label: 2, one vertical and one horizontal
options.feedback: Two suggests a vertical and a horizontal — but a circle has no preferred directions. Every diameter works equally.

options.label: 360, one line for every degree
options.feedback: 360 comes from counting one line per degree — but lines exist at every fraction of a degree too. The count outruns any number.

widget.prompt: A scalene triangle has three sides of three DIFFERENT lengths. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is the EQUILATERAL count — that fold works because the sides match. With three different lengths, every fold pairs unequal sides: none succeed.
Even one line would need two sides to trade places exactly — but no two sides here are equal, so every candidate fold overhangs.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Every fold must land a side on an equal side — impossible with all three different: 0.

hints: Run the fold test on each candidate — how many lines does each shape actually have?
The square gains folds a rectangle lacks; check its diagonals.
Square: 2 midlines + 2 diagonals. Which option says 4?
explanationVariants: The square has 4 lines: both midlines AND both diagonals (equal sides make the diagonal fold match). Rectangle 2, parallelogram 0, regular hexagon 6.
A square is a regular 4-gon, so it has exactly 4 lines — the regular-n-gon rule applied at n = 4.

widget.prompt: Which shape has EXACTLY 4 lines of symmetry?

options.label: a square
options.feedback: Two midlines plus two diagonals = 4 — the regular 4-gon gets its full n lines.

options.label: a (non-square) rectangle
options.feedback: The rectangle stops at 2 — its diagonal folds land long sides on short sides and fail.

options.label: a regular hexagon
options.feedback: Regular n-gon means n lines: the hexagon has 6, one more pair than asked for.

options.label: a parallelogram (no right angles)
options.feedback: A generic parallelogram has ZERO lines — every candidate fold mismatches the slanted sides. (Its symmetry is a different kind — next lesson.)

takeaways: Line symmetry = a reflection mapping the shape onto ITSELF; test by folding.
Regular n-gon: exactly n lines; circle: infinitely many; scalene: none.
Diagonals mirror the SQUARE but not the rectangle — the classic miscount.
steps.teaser: Next: symmetry by turning — shapes that come back to themselves before the turn is done.
